analysis.body:
The federal procurement record for defense AI work is public and consolidating. SAM.gov is the system of record for contract opportunities, awards, and subcontract reports, and the General Services Administration has retired the Electronic Subcontracting Reporting System and folded subcontracting reporting into SAM.gov. The FPDS.gov ezSearch feature has been retired and users are directed to SAM.gov for contract awards data searches, with the FPDS ATOM Feed to be retired later in FY 2026. USAspending carries award data built on the Federal Procurement Data System feed, so solicitations and awards can be traced directly without a subscription.

The Defense Innovation Unit describes itself as the Department's innovation pointman, with a mission to convert entrepreneurial products into tangible combat power. That is the stated commercial gateway where commercial AI enters DoD programs, and its project listings are public.

On what AI is actually deployed for, the material is thin but specific. Govini describes a platform layer that transforms activated data into adaptive workflows, mobilized agents, and AI-driven orchestration that proactively forecasts issues, prioritizes recommendations, and aligns resources, in the context of enterprise readiness. Janes describes applying advanced technology to connect millions of data points to uncover patterns, signals, and trajectories for decision-grade intelligence, including support for the Joint Intelligence Preparation of the Operational Environment process. These are the only deployment descriptions the sources provide.

Government labs occupy a distinct funding position. Per The World of AI, state-funded government labs carry public mandates and draw on sovereign budgets rather than venture capital or product revenue, which shapes what they build and why. The two verified entries, Technology Innovation Institute in Abu Dhabi and Shanghai AI Laboratory, can in principle command infrastructure commitments, including compute and facilities, that market-driven labs must negotiate for commercially.

On compliance, SAM.gov states that the system contains Controlled Unclassified Information and that all individuals viewing, reproducing, or disposing of this information are required to protect it in accordance with 32 CFR Part 2002 and GSA Order CIO 2103.2, with unauthorized activities subject to disciplinary action including criminal prosecution. The sources are silent on AI-specific risk frameworks and on ROI figures. A reader deciding whether to deploy should start with the free procurement record in SAM.gov and USAspending, treat the Defense Innovation Unit as the stated commercial entry point, and treat Govini and Janes as subscription analysts layered on top of that public record.

https://www.janes.com/.brief: Janes reports that it gathers information from vetted on-ground specialists, exclusive interviews, and events, acting as human sensors that web crawlers cannot reach. Janes reports that every data point is verified against reliable, vetted sources and that its dataset is the largest of its type, connecting millions of points to uncover patterns. Janes reports that its final content is peer reviewed to meet its quality and accuracy standards, and that it supplies validated data for the Joint Intelligence Preparation of the Operational Environment process. Janes reports that its digital portal lets users navigate validated data to uncover insights, moving from “what happened” to “what it means.”

https://www.govini.com/.brief: Govini says that Air is a leader in Enterprise Readiness and that its mission is to make readiness a real-time, continuously achieved condition. The company explains that its platform layer turns activated data into adaptive workflows, mobilized agents, and AI-driven orchestration that forecasts issues, prioritizes recommendations, and aligns resources.

https://theworldofai.org/ai-ecosystem/ec.brief: The World of AI's Government Labs page catalogues two verified organisations, Technology Innovation Institute and Shanghai AI Laboratory, each with a sourced classification note. It states that classifications are based on documents the organisations published about themselves, with the source and date recorded, rather than assigned by keyword or model. The page describes state-funded government labs as carrying public mandates and sovereign budgets, unlike venture-funded or product-driven labs. It notes TII operates under Abu Dhabi's Advanced Technology Research Council and has released frontier open models, while Shanghai AI Laboratory is backed by national ministries and municipal government. Both, according to the page, can command infrastructure commitments such as compute and facilities that market-driven labs must negotiate for commercially.
